source.title: No Free Lunch for Defending Against Prefilling Attack by In-Context Learning
source.authors: Zhi-Yu Xue; Guang-Da Liu; Bo-Cheng Chen; K. Johnson; Ramtin Pedarsani

record.tranche_reason: The study measures harmful-request attack success under prefilling across models and settings, using ASR rather than the original claim’s per-token KL measurement or fine-tuning intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper measures prefilling attacks and reports ASR for them. Its baseline means no ICL defense, not no prefilling; it does not report a paired no-prefill ASR in the extracted results. It also reports results for ICL defenses, combined attacks, and benign-query over-defense; those are not included here because they evaluate the paper’s defense method or a different outcome rather than the claim’s core prefilling attack result.
record.test_reason: The study measures prefilling-attack ASR (k=2–8 affirmative tokens) on safety-tuned open models across AdvBench, JailBench and SorryBench, which bears directly on V4. It reports no paired no-prefill ASR, so the size of the prefilling effect is inferred from absolute rates. ICL-defense results are the authors' own method and are not V4 evidence.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say current safety alignment fails to stop prefilling attacks. ICL demonstrations with adversative structure ('Sure... However, I cannot') robustly cut ASR across model sizes and combined attacks. But they cause over-defense on benign queries independent of model size, hence 'no free lunch'. They attribute this to a lack of adversative sentences in pretraining data.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates prefilling attacks and ICL-based defenses; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning intervention or per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR varies by model, benchmark, number of prefilling tokens, and evaluation judge. The paper says more prefilling tokens generally strengthen the attack and reports judge disagreements for some Llama models.
record.problems: The extracted ASR tables do not provide a paired no-prefill reference, so the size of the change caused by prefilling alone is not directly quantified here. Rule-based and model-based judges can disagree substantially for some Llama results. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row limit, omitted Table 1 ICL-defense-method results, Table 2 combined-attack results, and other prefill-length/judge tables (including Tables 4, 6, and 7); the selected rows retain Table 1 baseline attack results, the reported judge differences, and Table 5 model-based prefill-length results. Figure 2 safety-alignment comparisons and Table 4 over-defense outcomes were also not transcribed.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position-wise analysis.
No suffix-only or decoding-change attacks. Combined attacks (AIM, EC, RS) are prompt jailbreaks added to prefilling. No no-prefill control.
The authors speculate that a lack of adversative sentences in pretraining explains ICL over-defense, but they do not test it.
No training-based deepening. The adversative ICL defense is a prompting analogue, the authors' own method.

missing.what: Aligned (Vicuna-13B) vs unaligned (WizardLM-13B-Uncensored) ASR across prefill lengths. The authors claim safety alignment does not help against prefilling. Values are only in a figure, not in the text.
Baseline prefilling ASR at k=2/4/8 for the second benchmark set (labelled AdvBench but probably JailBench). Llama3.1-8b model-based ASR is 0, 0 and 10%; Llama2 k=2 is 0%.
Rule-based baseline ASR by prefill length.
Prefill combined with AIM/EC/RS baseline ASR, e.g. Llama3.1-8b model-based rises from 10% to 60–80%.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The main caveat for V4 is the missing no-prefill control. Several evaluated models are weakly aligned (Vicuna, Mistral v0.1), and falcon-11B is a base checkpoint despite the paper saying all models are safety-tuned. The authors also note Llama models resist small prefill lengths, consistent with ASR rising with prefilled tokens as in Qi et al.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.

No direct paired comparison with the same prompts without prefilling is reported in the extracted results. It tests affirmative prefilling, but not decoding changes; combined jailbreak prompts are not a test of suffixes specifically.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause shallow safety.
Training to deepen safety and its robustness.

relationships.condition: Falcon-7b-instruct, Vicuna-7b/13b, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1; any prefill length 2–8; model-based judge
relationships.reason: Prefilling yields 64–96% model-based ASR across benchmarks (R01-R03, R19-R27, R34-R36, R52-R60). These models have weak alignment and there is no no-prefill control.
relationships.display_finding: Model-judged attack success was 64–96% across benchmarks, but these models are weakly aligned and no no-prefill control was run.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Falcon-7b-instruct, Vicuna-7b/13b, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1; any prefill length 2–8; model-based judge
source_check.reason: R01–R03, R19–R27, R34–R36 and R52–R60 show 64.4–95.77% model-based ASR at tested lengths k=2,4,6,8. This supports successful compliance under prefilling, although no matched no-prefill comparison isolates its incremental effect.

relationships.condition: Strongly safety-tuned Llama2-chat / Llama3.x-Instruct, k≥4, model-based judge
relationships.reason: Prefilling only partly defeats refusal, with about 10–47% model-based ASR (R07-R18, R41-R42, R44-R48, R50-R51).
relationships.display_finding: Prefilling reached only about 10–47% attack success by the model-based judge, so it only partly defeated refusal.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Strongly safety-tuned Llama2-chat / Llama3.x-Instruct, k≥4, model-based judge
source_check.reason: The cited Llama results show incomplete bypass. The reason's 10–47% range needs correction to 10–60%: Table 1 includes 50.0% for Llama2-7b and 60.0% for Llama3.2-3b on JailBench.

relationships.condition: Llama models with only 2 prefilled tokens
relationships.reason: ASR stays near zero (0.19–1.73%; R40, R43, R49), so the bypass depends on prefill length.
relationships.display_finding: On Llama2-7b, Llama2-13b and Llama3.2-3b with 2 prefilled tokens, attack success stayed near zero (0.19–1.73%), so the bypass depends on prefill length.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Llama models with only 2 prefilled tokens
source_check.reason: R40, R43 and R49 give near-zero ASR of 0.19%, 0.19% and 1.73%; Appendix C explicitly says Llama models can defend against short prefills. These are failure conditions for bypass and warrant challenges. Narrow the condition to Llama2-7b/13b and Llama3.2-3b: Llama3.1-8b has 13.08% at k=2.

relationships.condition: Llama3.1-8b / Llama3.2-3b, rule-based vs model-based judge
relationships.reason: Rule-based ASR (57–80%, R28-R33) far exceeds model-based ASR (10–60%). Outputs lacking refusal often lack harmful content, so the measured bypass depends on the judge.
relationships.display_finding: Rule-based attack success (57–80%) far exceeded model-based success (10–60%), because outputs without a refusal often lacked harmful content.

source_check.reason: Table 1 gives rule-based ASR of 57.3–80.0% versus model-based ASR of 10.0–60.0%. Appendix C explains that affirmative responses without sufficient harmful information pass the rule-based criterion, establishing judge dependence.
